Assignment 07 / Sculpting for Design

Carving in Plaster of Paris

I carved an expressive face and a patterned pillar from Plaster of Paris.

Plaster of Paris · Carving

I used two plaster studies to explore expression and repeated pattern. Working with the material also taught me about timing: once the plaster had hardened, it was much more difficult to carve.

01

An expression in the eyes

For my smaller carving, I wanted to create a face. I drew on manga I had read as a child, particularly the way eye angles and eyebrows can convey a full expression.

I translated that idea into a compact three-dimensional form, using shallow cuts to establish the features. The different views show how the incisions sit on the curved plaster surface.

02

A lesson in timing

For the pillar, I tried simple carved patterns. I made the mistake of waiting too long after setting the plaster, and it had become quite hard to carve.

I was still satisfied with the result. The depth created by subtraction gave the surface an effect that reminded me of whittled wood. The repeating marks became part of the piece’s character.

03

Expression and pattern

I used the same subtractive process for two different purposes: suggesting a facial expression and developing a sequence of geometric and curved patterns around a taller form.

I photographed both studies to show the depth of the cuts and the way light and shadow describe the carved surfaces.

04

Learning from the material

Waiting too long after setting made the pillar difficult to work with. This taught me how much the material’s changing hardness can affect the carving process.

I remained satisfied with the whittled-wood effect created by the cuts. These pieces record both my finished forms and my practical experience of working with plaster.

The original pages.

This shared submission documents the plaster face and pillar on pages 3–4; the foam study has its own project page.
